```{r setup}
source(here::here("R", "prior_fig.R"))
```

These figures reconstruct and extend the prior figure from the
louseplague project (`figure/prior_fig.R` there), adding the sources
compiled here. Each panel is one parameter, on the canonical scale in
`data/param_dict.csv`: durations in days and rates per day.

- **Panel titles** give the parameter's description, then its symbol
  and units.
- **Rows** are sources. From bottom to top: literature values compiled
  by Park, our own extractions, @keeling2000bubonic and
  @didelot2017model. The yersinia scenario values are left out by
  default ([see below](#yersinia-scenarios)). Rows are labelled with abbreviated references built from
  the bibliography: the first four letters of the first author's
  surname, then those of the second author (two authors) or `+` (three
  or more), then the year, e.g. `KeelGill2000`, `Toll+2010`. The
  Indian Plague Commission is `IPC1908`.
- **Several values in one row** are spread vertically, beeswarm-style,
  only where they would otherwise overlap; an interval moves together
  with its estimate. The layout is deterministic (no random jitter).
- **Colour** shows the source.
- **Shape** shows the kind of value:
  - point estimate;
  - range;
  - CI, either reported or derived from mean ± SD or SE;
  - posterior mean with 95% credible interval;
  - a value fixed (assumed) by a modelling study;
  - a *maximum*, i.e. the longest duration observed. A maximum is a
    bound, not a mean (see `data/README.md`).
- **Curves** at the bottom of each panel are prior densities, each
  scaled to the same height. The louseplague priors (Park et al., see
  [below](#louseplague-priors)) are filled grey areas. yersinia's
  `prior_default()` priors are dashed blue lines and its
  `plague_fit_prior()` priors are dotted. yersinia priors on rates are
  transformed to durations where needed (e.g. 1/`m_r`).

KG values that don't mean the same thing as the literature parameter
are left out: KG's search efficiency *a* (vs. Dean et al.'s $s_f$) and
KG's $\beta_H$ (vs. Dean et al.'s $\beta_b$). Values that a study took
from an earlier model are also left out, since they duplicate the
original (`borrowed_from` in the data). These are Didelot et al.'s
fixed rat infectious period (18 days) and human recovery probability
(0.1), both from KG. The figures are built by
`make` as `outputs/figs/param_priors_{lit,model,lit_ratflea}.{pdf,png}`.
`make tikz` writes LaTeX versions. `prior_fig()` can also show a subset
of parameters by transmission mode (`include_modes`, `exclude_modes`:
rat-flea, human-ecto, pneumonic) or host/vector (`include_hosts`,
`exclude_hosts`: rat, human, flea, louse), using the `mode` and `host`
columns of `data/param_dict.csv`.

### yersinia scenario values {#yersinia-scenarios}

The yersinia package has five parameter sets (`inst/scenarios/*.yaml`,
all per day, in Didelot's carcass formulation). We leave them out of
the figures, because the aim is to get as close as possible to primary
sources:

- `didelot` and `keeling-gilligan` restate @didelot2017model's and
  KG's values, converted to the carcass model, e.g. ρ = *a*·*K_R* and
  δ_R = *d_F* for KG. They duplicate rows already in the figures.
- `historical` and `modern-estimates` cite no specific sources
  ("historical analysis and paleoepidemiology", "multiple contemporary
  sources"). Their values look like round-number adjustments of the
  KG/Didelot values, with qualitative reasons.
- `defaults` is a curated starting point for fitting. The package's
  `explainer/parameters.html` gives a short rationale for each value
  but no references.

`prior_fig(..., scenarios = TRUE)` adds them back, as crosses in a
"yersinia scenarios" row. yersinia's *prior* curves are still shown.

## How the louseplague priors were derived {#louseplague-priors}

Park et al. describe their method in the louseplague manuscript
(`doc/plague.Rnw` in that repository, "To construct informative
priors ..." and Table `tab:param`). The priors themselves are in
`data/louseplague_priors.csv`.

- Literature values were collected and plotted (the original version of
  these figures). A prior was then **chosen for each parameter
  separately**, a Gamma for positive parameters and a Beta for
  probabilities. Each prior was chosen so that its high-density region
  contains most of the reported values. The manuscript describes no
  fitting procedure, so the priors seem to have been chosen by eye.
- The priors are **independent**, "for convenience", even though some
  parameters (e.g. transmission rates and infectious periods) are
  probably correlated.
- Some values were **left out as implausible** compared with the other
  studies:
  - the rat infectious period ($1/\gamma_r$ = 18.25 days) assumed by
    @keeling2000metapopulation;
  - the incubation and infectious periods reported by
    @scott2001biology. The manuscript calls these $1/\sigma_r$ and
    $1/\gamma_r$, but the Scott & Duncan values in Park's compilation
    are for human bubonic plague [($1/\sigma_b$]{style="white-space: nowrap;"}
    and [$1/\gamma_b$)]{style="white-space: nowrap;"}, so those are
    probably the ones meant.
- When a parameter has **only one reported value**, the prior spans a
  "biologically realistic range" around it. For example,
  @evans1952intrinsic estimated the louse growth rate as 0.111/day
  (doubling time 6.2 days). The prior's 95% range is 0.05–0.17/day,
  i.e. doubling times of 4.1–14.5 days.
- **Rat-to-human ratio:** @didelot2017model and @dean2018human assume
  one susceptible rat per susceptible human. The prior relaxes this to
  a Gamma with mean 1 and 95% range of about 0.3–2.
- **Transmission rates** ($\beta_p$, $\beta_b$, $\beta_r$, $\beta_h$,
  $\beta_l$): @dean2018human used uniform priors. These are replaced
  by Gamma priors with the same means and shape 2.

The values in the "only one value" and "relaxed" cases set the location
of the prior, but its width is a judgement call. The plotted
literature values therefore don't fully determine these priors.

```{r louseplague-prior-table}
dict <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "param_dict.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
lp <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "louseplague_priors.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
lp <- lp[order(match(lp$param, dict$param)), ]
q <- \(p) ifelse(lp$family == "Gamma",
                 qgamma(p, shape = lp$shape, scale = lp$scale),
                 qbeta(p, lp$shape1, lp$shape2))
fmt <- \(x) format_num(x)
tab <- data.frame(
    parameter = dict$description[match(lp$param, dict$param)],
    symbol = paste0("$", dict$label[match(lp$param, dict$param)], "$"),
    prior = ifelse(lp$family == "Gamma",
                   sprintf("Gamma(shape = %s, scale = %s)", lp$shape, lp$scale),
                   sprintf("Beta(%s, %s)", lp$shape1, lp$shape2)),
    mean = fmt(ifelse(lp$family == "Gamma", lp$shape * lp$scale,
                      lp$shape1 / (lp$shape1 + lp$shape2))),
    `95% range` = paste0(fmt(q(0.025)), "–", fmt(q(0.975))),
    units = lp$units,
    check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "louseplague priors (Park et al.), with means and central 95% ranges.")
```

## Parameters with literature values

The panels cover the 22 parameters in louseplague's figure.

```{r fig-lit, fig.width = 16, fig.height = 15, out.width = "100%"}
prior_fig("lit")
```

### Rat and flea parameters only

The same figure without parameters involving humans or lice
(`exclude_hosts = c("human", "louse")`).

```{r fig-lit-ratflea, fig.width = 16, fig.height = 8, out.width = "100%"}
prior_fig("lit", exclude_hosts = c("human", "louse"))
```

## Parameters set only by models

KG, Didelot et al. and yersinia specify these parameters, but we have no
literature values for them yet. They include rat and human demography,
movement rates, the carcass-model parameters and rat $R_0$. The x axes
are logarithmic, and zero values are omitted (e.g. the `didelot`
scenario's `r_r = d_r = 0`).

```{r fig-model, fig.width = 16, fig.height = 8, out.width = "100%"}
prior_fig("model")
```
